    Chapter 15

    Secure Connections: SSH, VPNs, Wi-Fi and DNS

    🤔 SSH, VPNs, Wi-Fi and DNS look like four different worlds. Underneath, they’re the same handful of building blocks snapped together in different shapes.

    • ⏱️ ~8 min
    • 📚 4 sections
    • ⭐ 150 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    15.1SSH: secure remote access#

    SSH (Secure Shell) lets you log in to and control a remote computer over an encrypted connection. Developers and system administrators use it constantly: managing servers, copying files (scp, sftp), pushing code to GitHub, and creating encrypted tunnels. It runs on TCP port 22.

    📜 Origin story: in 1995, Finnish researcher Tatu Ylönen's university network was hit by a password-sniffing attack. The tools of the time (Telnet, rlogin) sent passwords in plain text. He wrote SSH to replace them, and within a few years it had replaced them almost everywhere.

    How an SSH connection works

    Step 4 is "trust on first use" (TOFU). SSH has no certificate authority by default. The first time you connect to a server, you see:

    If you answer "yes," SSH saves the server's public key in ~/.ssh/known_hosts. Next time, it checks the key matches. If it ever changes, you get a loud warning:

    That could be harmless (the server was reinstalled) or a man-in-the-middle attack. Check with the server's administrator before continuing. Ideally, verify the fingerprint through another channel the very first time, too.

    Step 5: key-based login is safer than passwords. Your public key goes in the server's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file. When you log in, your SSH client signs data unique to this session with your private key, and the server verifies it with your public key. Your private key never leaves your laptop, so there's nothing for a fake server to steal.

    Larger organizations often use SSH certificates: an internal SSH CA signs user and host keys, which removes the "trust on first use" prompt and makes revoking access easy.

    SSH's modern algorithms

    Run ssh -Q kex to see the key exchanges your SSH supports. Recent OpenSSH versions (10.0 and later) use the post-quantum hybrid mlkem768x25519-sha256 by default, with curve25519-sha256 as a fallback. For encryption, they use chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com or AES-GCM.

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    # Create a modern SSH key pair (you'll be asked for a passphrase: use one!)
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "alice@laptop"
# Creates ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      (PRIVATE: never share)
#     and ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub  (PUBLIC: give this to servers, GitHub, etc.)

cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
# ssh-ed25519 AAAAC3NzaC1lZDI1NTE5AAAAI... alice@laptop

# Show your key's fingerprint
ssh-keygen -lf ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# Install your public key on a server you can already log in to
ssh-copy-id user@server.example

# Watch the algorithm negotiation in detail
ssh -v user@server.example 2>&1 | grep -iE "kex: algorithm|host key algorithm|cipher"

# Load your key into the SSH agent so you type the passphrase only once per session
ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519

    For extra protection, you can keep SSH keys on a hardware security key: ssh-keygen -t ed25519-sk creates a key that requires a physical touch on a FIDO2 device (like a YubiKey) for every login.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    SSH authentication

    ❌ Avoid
    Password login

    Type a password

    • Nothing to set up
    • Brute-forced by bots 24/7
    • Phishable, reusable
    Best for: Disable on servers
    ✅ Use it
    Ed25519 key

    ssh-keygen -t ed25519

    • Can’t be guessed; short keys
    • Works with agents
    • Private key file must be protected with a passphrase
    Best for: Everyday SSH
    ✅ Use it
    ed25519-sk (hardware)

    Key lives on a YubiKey

    • Private key can’t be copied off the device
    • Requires a physical touch
    • Need the device with you; buy a backup
    Best for: Admins and high-value servers
    ✅ Use it
    SSH certificates

    A CA signs user/host keys

    • No TOFU prompts; short-lived access
    • You need to run an SSH CA
    Best for: Larger fleets

    15.2VPNs: encrypted tunnels#

    A VPN (Virtual Private Network) wraps all your network traffic in an encrypted tunnel to a VPN server, which then forwards it to the internet.

    Common uses:

    • Remote work: connect to a company's internal network from home.
    • Site-to-site: link two office networks over the internet.
    • Public Wi-Fi: stop the local network from seeing your traffic.
    • Changing your apparent location: websites see the VPN server's IP address.

    What a VPN does and doesn't do:

    ✅ A VPN does ❌ A VPN does not
    Hide your traffic from the local network and your internet provider Hide your traffic from the VPN provider, who can now see what your internet provider used to see
    Hide your real IP address from websites Make you anonymous (logins, cookies and browser fingerprints still identify you)
    Protect unencrypted protocols on untrusted networks Protect you from phishing, malware or bad passwords
    Give access to private networks Replace HTTPS (you still need it after the VPN server)

    VPN protocols:

    Protocol Layer Crypto Notes
    WireGuard Network Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s, HKDF (the Noise protocol framework) ✅ Modern, fast, about 4,000 lines of code. Built into Linux since 2020. Basis of Tailscale and many commercial VPNs.
    IPsec (IKEv2 + ESP) Network AES-GCM, ECDH, certificates or pre-shared keys ✅ Built into most operating systems and routers; complex to configure
    OpenVPN Application (TLS-based) TLS 1.2/1.3 ✅ Flexible, widely supported, slower
    L2TP/IPsec Network IPsec ⚠️ Legacy
    PPTP — MS-CHAPv2, RC4 ❌ Broken; never use

    WireGuard's design is interesting because it has no algorithm negotiation. Every connection uses the same fixed, modern algorithms. That removes a whole class of "downgrade" attacks, where an attacker tricks both sides into using weaker options. If the algorithms ever need changing, the protocol version changes.

    Each WireGuard device has a key pair, much like SSH. A client configuration looks like this:

    Config
    [Interface]
PrivateKey = <this device's private key>
Address    = 10.0.0.2/32

[Peer]
PublicKey  = <the server's public key>
Endpoint   = vpn.example.com:51820
AllowedIPs = 0.0.0.0/0          # send all traffic through the tunnel
    Terminal
    # Generate a WireGuard key pair (requires wireguard-tools)
wg genkey | tee privatekey | wg pubkey > publickey
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    VPN protocols

    ✅ Use it
    WireGuard

    ~4,000 lines, fixed modern crypto

    • Tiny, fast, easy to audit
    • No negotiation → no downgrades
    • UDP only
    • Static IP assignments need extra tooling
    Best for: Most new VPNs
    ✅ Use it
    IPsec / IKEv2

    Network layer standard

    • Built into every OS and router
    • Great for site-to-site
    • Complex configuration
    • Huge spec
    Best for: Enterprise and mobile
    👍 Situational
    OpenVPN

    TLS-based

    • Flexible; works over TCP 443
    • Slower; large code base
    Best for: Restrictive networks
    ⚠️ Legacy
    L2TP/IPsec

    Older combo

    • Widely supported
    • Double encapsulation; often weak pre-shared keys
    Best for: Legacy clients
    ❌ Avoid
    PPTP

    MS-CHAPv2 + RC4

    • Ancient and easy
    • Completely broken
    Best for: Never
    ✔ section read

    15.3Wi-Fi security#

    Wi-Fi is radio. Anyone within range, including someone in a car outside, can capture every packet. Wi-Fi encryption protects the hop between your device and the access point (router).

    Standard Year Encryption Status
    Open network — None ❌ Anyone nearby can read unencrypted traffic
    WEP 1997 RC4 with a tiny 24-bit IV that repeats ❌ Crackable in minutes
    WPA (TKIP) 2003 Patched RC4, as a stopgap ❌ Obsolete
    WPA2 2004 AES-CCMP ⚠️ OK with a strong password; weaknesses below
    WPA3 2018 AES with SAE key exchange ✅ Use it if your devices support it
    Enhanced Open (OWE) 2018 Encryption on open networks, no password ✅ Better than open; protects against passive snooping

    WPA2-Personal and the 4-way handshake

    With a home Wi-Fi password (a "pre-shared key"):

    1. Both your device and the router turn the password into a 256-bit key, the PMK (Pairwise Master Key), using PBKDF2 (Chapter 8) with the network name (SSID) as the salt and 4,096 iterations.
    2. When you connect, they perform a 4-way handshake: they exchange fresh random numbers (nonces) and each derives a temporary session key, the PTK, from the PMK, both nonces and both devices' hardware addresses. Each side proves it knows the PMK with a MIC (a MAC) without ever sending the password.

    WPA2-Personal's weaknesses:

    • Offline password guessing: an attacker who records a handshake (or forces your device to reconnect) can try millions of passwords per second on their own computer, checking each guess against the captured MIC. Short or common Wi-Fi passwords fall quickly.
    • No forward secrecy: anyone who knows the Wi-Fi password and captured your handshake can decrypt your traffic.
    • 📜 KRACK (2017): researchers showed that by replaying handshake messages, an attacker could make devices reinstall a key and reset nonces, causing nonce reuse. It was fixed with software updates.

    WPA3 and SAE

    WPA3-Personal replaces the 4-way handshake's password step with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), also called "Dragonfly." It's a PAKE (password-authenticated key exchange, Chapter 17): a Diffie-Hellman-style exchange woven together with the password.

    • Offline guessing is no longer possible. Each password guess requires a live exchange with the router.
    • Forward secrecy: learning the password later doesn't decrypt past traffic.

    (Some early WPA3 implementations had flaws, known as "Dragonblood" (2019), which were patched.)

    Enterprise Wi-Fi

    Companies and universities use WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise (802.1X). Each person logs in with their own username and password or certificate, checked by a central server (RADIUS) through a method like EAP-TLS. The worldwide university network eduroam works this way.

    ⚠️ Watch out: on enterprise Wi-Fi, your device must check the login server's certificate. If it doesn't, an attacker can set up an "evil twin" access point with the same name and collect people's passwords.

    Wi-Fi checklist for your home: use WPA3 (or WPA2-AES if needed), a long random passphrase, turn off WPS (its 8-digit PIN can be brute-forced), and keep the router's firmware updated.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Wi-Fi security

    ❌ Avoid
    Open

    No encryption

    • Easy to join
    • Anyone nearby reads unencrypted traffic
    Best for: Only with HTTPS/VPN on top
    ❌ Avoid
    WEP

    RC4 + 24-bit IV

    • None today
    • Cracked in minutes
    Best for: Never
    ❌ Avoid
    WPA (TKIP)

    Patched RC4 stopgap

    • Was better than WEP
    • Obsolete
    Best for: Never
    👍 Situational
    WPA2-AES

    AES-CCMP, 4-way handshake

    • Supported by every device
    • Captured handshakes allow offline guessing
    • KRACK (patched)
    Best for: Old devices, with a long passphrase
    ✅ Use it
    WPA3 (SAE)

    Dragonfly PAKE

    • No offline guessing
    • Forward secrecy
    • Older devices can’t join
    • Early Dragonblood bugs (patched)
    Best for: Every home and office
    ✅ Use it
    Enterprise (802.1X)

    Per-user login via RADIUS

    • Individual credentials; easy revocation
    • Devices must check the server certificate (evil twins!)
    Best for: Companies and universities (eduroam)
    ✔ section read

    15.4DNS security: DNSSEC, DoT and DoH#

    Remember the two problems with DNS from Chapter 12: no authenticity (fake answers) and no privacy (everyone sees your lookups). There's a separate fix for each.

    DNSSEC: signed DNS answers (authenticity)

    DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS records. Each zone (like example.com) signs its records with its own key, and the parent zone (.com) vouches for that key, all the way up to the root zone, whose key is the trust anchor built into resolvers.

    It's a chain of trust, like certificates, but for DNS. DNSSEC protects against forged answers. It does not encrypt anything: everyone can still see your queries.

    📜 The root key ceremony: the root zone's signing key is managed in highly scripted public ceremonies, held in secure facilities in the US, where a group of trusted community representatives from around the world each bring part of what's needed to access the key's hardware. The ceremonies are filmed and streamed.

    🧪 Try it yourself:

    Terminal
    # Ask a validating resolver for a signed answer
dig +dnssec cloudflare.com A @1.1.1.1
# cloudflare.com.  254  IN  A      104.16.132.229
# cloudflare.com.  254  IN  RRSIG  A 13 2 300 ...   ← the signature (algorithm 13 = ECDSA P-256)
#
# ;; flags: qr rd ra ad;   ← "ad" = Authenticated Data: the resolver validated the signature

    DNS over TLS and DNS over HTTPS (privacy)

    DoT (DNS over TLS, port 853) and DoH (DNS over HTTPS, port 443) wrap DNS queries in TLS, so the local network and your internet provider can't see or tamper with them. Your chosen resolver (for example 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8 or 9.9.9.9) still sees your queries, so you're moving trust rather than eliminating it. Modern browsers and operating systems support both.

    Plain DNS DNSSEC DoT / DoH
    Detects forged answers ❌ ✅ (end to end, from the domain owner) ✅ (between you and the resolver only)
    Hides your queries from the local network ❌ ❌ ✅
    Who must deploy it — Domain owners and resolvers You (or your browser/OS) and the resolver

    They work well together: DNSSEC proves the answer is genuine; DoH/DoT keeps the question private.

    Terminal
    # Ask Cloudflare's resolver over HTTPS
curl -s -H 'accept: application/dns-json' \
  'https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query?name=example.com&type=A'
# {"Status":0, ..., "AD":true, ..., "Answer":[{"name":"example.com","type":1,"TTL":297,"data":"172.66.147.243"}, ...]}
    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    DNS security

    👍 Situational
    DNSSEC

    Signed answers

    • Detects forged DNS answers
    • Enables DANE
    • No privacy
    • Complex; outages from expired signatures
    Best for: Authenticity of DNS data
    ✅ Use it
    DNS over TLS (DoT)

    Port 853

    • Encrypts lookups
    • Easy for networks to manage
    • Dedicated port is easy to block
    Best for: Phones (Android Private DNS), routers
    ✅ Use it
    DNS over HTTPS (DoH)

    Looks like normal HTTPS

    • Encrypts lookups; hard to block
    • Moves trust to the resolver provider
    • Hides DNS from network admins
    Best for: Browsers
